FIELD NOTE / 002 · PUBLIC INTEREST

A seat at the table.
A say in the outcome.

Public participation should shape the decision—not just appear in the consultation summary.

ILLUSTRATIVE SAMPLE3 MIN READ

This sample was prepared for the portfolio website. It is not a prior publication or a claim about Jia’s professional work.

Imagine a city considering an AI tool to help allocate a public service. It hosts a consultation after choosing the vendor, setting the budget, and agreeing on a launch date. Residents are invited to comment, but the decisions they care about may already be difficult to change.

This hypothetical example points to a basic design problem: participation needs both an invitation and room to influence the outcome. The following questions offer a way to examine whether that room exists.

What is still open to change?

A consultation brief should say which decisions participants can influence. Is the institution asking whether AI is appropriate at all, which safeguards are needed, or only how a finished service should be explained?

Each question can be useful. Confusing them creates expectations that the process cannot meet. A team could publish a simple decision map: what is fixed, what is open, who will decide, and when.

Whose experience is missing?

An open invitation does not automatically produce a representative conversation. Timing, language, compensation, disability access, and familiarity with technical language all affect who can take part.

For the imagined public service, this could mean reaching people who have difficulty applying, not only those who already use the service successfully. Participation should not require people to become AI specialists before their experience counts.

The test is not only who was heard, but what their contribution could change.

How will the institution respond?

Before gathering input, decide how it will be considered and how participants will hear back. A response can identify proposals adopted, proposals declined and why, and issues needing more evidence. Disagreement should remain visible rather than disappearing into a broad statement of consensus.

In this proposed approach, a public response record is part of the process itself. It creates a trail between a person’s contribution and an institution’s choice.

Participation after launch

People may discover problems only after a service becomes part of daily life. A continuing feedback route, with a named owner and a review schedule, can help an institution learn from that experience. A launch date should not also be the end of listening.

The OECD AI Principles place human rights and democratic values within the AI lifecycle. The process ideas here are one illustrative way to ask what that commitment could mean in practice.

SOURCES & CONTEXT

OECD · AI Principles ↗

The city example is hypothetical. The participation design questions are proposals for discussion, not findings from an actual consultation.
